original_value: AbstractDevOps as a new way of thinking for software development and operations has received much attention in the industry, while it has not been thoroughly investigated in academia yet. The objective of this study is to characterize DevOps by exploring its central components in terms of principles, practices and their relations to the principles, challenges of DevOps adoption, and benefits reported in the peer‐reviewed literature. As a key objective, we also aim to realize the relations between DevOps practices and benefits in a systematic manner. A systematic literature review was conducted. Also, we used the concept of benefits dependency network to synthesize the findings, in particular, to specify dependencies between DevOps practices and link the practices to benefits. We found that in many cases, DevOps characteristics, ie, principles, practices, benefits, and challenges, were not sufficiently defined in detail in the peer‐reviewed literature. In addition, only a few empirical studies are available, which can be attributed to the nascency of DevOps research. Also, an initial version of the DevOps benefits dependency network has been derived. The definition of DevOps principles and practices should be emphasized given the novelty of the concept. Further empirical studies are needed to improve the benefits dependency network presented in this study.

result.paraphrase: AbstractDevOps, a new perspective on software development and operations, has drawn significant industry attention, yet it has not been extensively studied in academia. This study aims to characterize DevOps by examining its core elements—principles, practices, their links to principles, adoption challenges, and benefits reported in the peer-reviewed literature. A further goal is to systematically clarify the relationships between DevOps practices and benefits. We conducted a systematic literature review and used the benefits dependency network concept to synthesize the findings, specifically to define dependencies among DevOps practices and connect practices to benefits. We found that, in many cases, DevOps characteristics such as principles, practices, benefits, and challenges are not described in sufficient detail in the peer-reviewed literature. In addition, only a few empirical studies are available, reflecting the early stage of DevOps research. An initial DevOps benefits dependency network was also developed. Given the novelty of DevOps, its principles and practices should be defined more clearly, and further empirical research is needed to refine the benefits dependency network presented here.
